chapter_theme: A song at Nedungalam (நெடுங்களம்): the poet asks that the senses, past deeds and diseases burn like cotton, that he live among the old devotees, and that Murugan come on the peacock and give his feet; the praise describes Murugan's own lovemaking with his consort.

892.reading: The poet asks that the five senses, the two old deeds and diseases burn to ash like cotton, that he live among the old servants of the Lord, and that Murugan, with the elephant-faced one, come on the peacock with anklets sounding bindu and nada, kill his care and give the full feet today. The praise describes the union of Murugan with his golden consort, waist and eyes whirling, garments slipping, the moon-brow and dark hair tumbling, and names him the lord of Nedungalam, where devotees gather and Brahma and the gods praise him.
892.nuance: The frank love scene here belongs to the god, not to the poet's confession: மங்கை மணமுண்ட பாலா. பழைய தொண்டர்களுடன் பழகி asks for the company of the old devotees. சிலம்பு கழல் விந்து நாதம்: the anklets sound as bindu and nada. பஞ்சவர் வியன் பதியுடன் குலாவ is obscure; it may name the five (the senses, or Siva's five faces).

links.note: 892 asks that the five senses, the two old deeds and diseases burn to ash like cotton (பஞ்செனஎரிந்து பொடியங்கமாகி) when Murugan comes and gives his feet. Tirumanthiram 117 says the sunstone burns the cotton around it only in the sun's presence (சூரியன் சந்நிதியிற் சுடுமாறு), and so the malas end when the Lord appears. Both use burning cotton for impurity destroyed at once, and both make the destruction wait on the Lord's coming.
